entries.ec57ca9cd292197f6b1454929fbb222dd903416b: <div sID="gen8481" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="34" osisID="2Chr.34" sID="2Chr.34"/> <div eID="gen8481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8482" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8483" type="x-p"/> Before we see Judah and Jerusalem ruined we shall yet see some glorious years, while good Josiah sits at the helm. By his pious endeavours for reformation God tried them yet once more; if they had known in this their day, the day of their visitation, the things that belonged to their peace and improved them, their ruin might have been prevented. But after this reign they were hidden from their eyes, and the next reigns brought an utter desolation upon them. In this chapter we have, I. A general account of Josiah's character, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.1-2Chr.34.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. His zeal to root out idolatry, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.3-2Chr.34.7">ver. 3-7</reference>. III. His care to repair the temple, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.8-2Chr.34.13">ver. 8-13</reference>. IV. The finding of the book of the law and the good use made of it, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.14-2Chr.34.28">ver. 14-28</reference>. V. The public reading of the law to the people and their renewing their covenant with God thereupon, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.29-2Chr.34.33">ver. 29-33</reference>. Much of this we had <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.1-2Kgs.22.20">2 Kings xxii.</reference>
entries.5c3ee724e984ed79405a0081292acdc4cb488f0a: <div eID="gen8483" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8482" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Reign of Josiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 623.)</title> <div sID="gen8484" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Josiah <hi type="italic">was</hi> eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem one and thirty years. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> right in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and walked in the ways of David his father, and declined <hi type="italic">neither</hi> to the right hand, nor to the left. <hi type="super">3</hi> For in the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet young, he began to seek after the God of David his father: and in the twelfth year he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem from the high places, and the groves, and the carved images, and the molten images. <hi type="super">4</hi> And they brake down the altars of Baalim in his presence; and the images, that <hi type="italic">were</hi> on high above them, he cut down; and the groves, and the carved images, and the molten images, he brake in pieces, and made dust <hi type="italic">of them,</hi> and strowed <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the graves of them that had sacrificed unto them. <hi type="super">5</hi> And he burnt the bones of the priests upon their altars, and cleansed Judah and Jerusalem. <hi type="super">6</hi> And <hi type="italic">so did he</hi> in the cities of Manasseh, and Ephraim, and Simeon, even unto Naphtali, with their mattocks round about. <hi type="super">7</hi> And when he had broken down the altars and the groves, and had beaten the graven images into powder, and cut down all the idols throughout all the land of Israel, he returned to Jerusalem. <div eID="gen8484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8485" type="x-p"/> Concerning Josiah we are here told, 1. That he came to the crown when he was very young, only eight years old (yet his infancy did not debar him from his right), and he reigned <hi type="italic">thirty-one years</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.1">v. 1</reference>), a considerable time. I fear, however, that in the beginning of his reign things went much as they had done in his father's time, because, being a child, he must have left the management of them to others; so that it was not till his twelfth year, which goes far in the number of his years, that the reformation began, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.3">v. 3</reference>. He could not, as Hezekiah did, fall about it immediately. 2. That he reigned very well (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.2">v. 2</reference>), approved himself to God, trod in the steps of David, and did not decline either <hi type="italic">to the right hand of to the left:</hi> for there are errors on both hands. 3. That while he was young, about sixteen years old, he <hi type="italic">began to seek after God,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.3">v. 3</reference>. We have reason to think he had not so good an education as Manasseh had (it is well if those about him did not endeavour to corrupt and debauch him); yet he thus sought God when he was young. It is the duty and interest of young people, and will particularly be the honour of young gentlemen, as soon as they come to years of understanding, to <hi type="italic">begin to seek God;</hi> for those that seek him early shall find him. 4. That in the twelfth year of his reign, when it is probable he took the administration of the government entirely into his own hands, he <hi type="italic">began to purge his kingdom from the remains of idolatry;</hi> he destroyed the high places, groves, images, altars, all the utensils of idolatry, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.3-2Chr.34.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. He not only cast them out as Manasseh did, but broke them to pieces, and made dust of them. This destruction of idolatry is here said to be in his twelfth year, but it was said (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.23">2 Kings xxiii. 23</reference>) to be in his eighteenth year. Something was probably done towards it in his twelfth year; then he began to purge out idolatry, but that good work met with opposition, so that it was not thoroughly done till they had found the book of the law six years afterwards. But here the whole work is laid together briefly which was much more largely and particularly related in the <hi type="italic">Kings.</hi> His zeal carried him out to do this, not only in Judah and Jerusalem, but in the cities of Israel too, as far as he had any influence upon them.
entries.1ab8eaebfeb7ef749c9eea32b0ec5f3783ceef3c: <div eID="gen8485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8486" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, when he had purged the land, and the house, he sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, and Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah the son of Joahaz the recorder, to repair the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God. <hi type="super">9</hi> And when they came to Hilkiah the high priest, they delivered the money that was brought into the house of God, which the Levites that kept the doors had gathered of the hand of Manasseh and Ephraim, and of all the remnant of Israel, and of all Judah and Benjamin; and they returned to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">10</hi> And they put <hi type="italic">it</hi> in the hand of the workmen that had the oversight of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and they gave it to the workmen that wrought in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to repair and amend the house: <hi type="super">11</hi> Even to the artificers and builders gave they <hi type="italic">it,</hi> to buy hewn stone, and timber for couplings, and to floor the houses which the kings of Judah had destroyed. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the men did the work faithfully: and the overseers of them <hi type="italic">were</hi> Jahath and Obadiah, the Levites, of the sons of Merari; and Zechariah and Meshullam, of the sons of the Kohathites, to set <hi type="italic">it</hi> forward; and <hi type="italic">other of</hi> the Levites, all that could skill of instruments of music. <hi type="super">13</hi> Also <hi type="italic">they were</hi> over the bearers of burdens, and <hi type="italic">were</hi> overseers of all that wrought the work in any manner of service: and of the Levites <hi type="italic">there were</hi> scribes, and officers, and porters. <div eID="gen8486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8487" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. Orders are given by the king for the repair of the temple, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.8">v. 8</reference>. When he had purged the house of the corruptions of it he began to fit it up for the services that were to be performed in it. Thus we must do by the spiritual temple of the heart, get it cleansed from the pollutions of sin, and then renewed, so as to be transformed into the image of God. Josiah, in this order, calls God <hi type="italic">the Lord his God.</hi> Those that truly love God will <hi type="italic">love the habitation of his house.</hi> 2. Care is taken about it, effectual care. The Levites went about the country and gathered money towards it, which was returned to the three trustees mentioned, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.8">v. 8</reference>. They brought it to Hilkiah the high priest (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.9">v. 9</reference>), and he and they put it into the hands of workmen, both overseers and labourers, who undertook to do it by the great, as we say, or <hi type="italic">in the gross,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.10-2Chr.34.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. It is observed that the workmen were industrious and honest: They <hi type="italic">did the work faithfully</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.12">v. 12</reference>); and workmen are not completely faithful if they are not both careful and diligent, for a confidence is reposed in them that they will be so. It is also intimated that the overseers were ingenious; for it is said that all those were employed to inspect this work who were skilful in <hi type="italic">instruments of music;</hi> not that their skill in music could be of any use in architecture, but it was an evidence that they were men of sense and ingenuity, and particularly that their genius lay towards the mathematics, which qualified them very much for this trust. Witty men are then wise men when they employ their wit in doing good, in helping their friends, and, as they have opportunity, in serving the public. Observe, in this work, how God dispenses his gifts variously; here were some that were <hi type="italic">bearers of burdens,</hi> cut out for bodily labour and fit to work. Here were others (made <hi type="italic">meliori luto—of finer materials</hi>) that had skill in music, and they were <hi type="italic">overseers of those that laboured,</hi> and scribes and officers. The former were the hands: these were the heads. They had need of one another, and the work needed both. Let not the overseers of the work despise the bearers of burdens, nor let those that work in the service grudge at those whose office it is to direct; but let each esteem and serve the other in love, and let God have the glory and the church the benefit of the different gifts and dispositions of both.
entries.2d48620d4a3b05ff6d792b58eb0cfcb93f6e366c: <div eID="gen8487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8488" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And when they brought out the money that was brought into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Hilkiah the priest found a book of the law of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">given</hi> by Moses. <hi type="super">15</hi> And Hilkiah answered and said to Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . And Hilkiah delivered the book to Shaphan. <hi type="super">16</hi> And Shaphan carried the book to the king, and brought the king word back again, saying, All that was committed to thy servants, they do <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">17</hi> And they have gathered together the money that was found in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and have delivered it into the hand of the overseers, and to the hand of the workmen. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then Shaphan the scribe told the king, saying, Hilkiah the priest hath given me a book. And Shaphan read it before the king. <hi type="super">19</hi> And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the law, that he rent his clothes. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the king commanded Hilkiah, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Abdon the son of Micah, and Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah a servant of the king's, saying, <hi type="super">21</hi> Go, enquire of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for me, and for them that are left in Israel and in Judah, concerning the words of the book that is found: for great <hi type="italic">is</hi> the wrath of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that is poured out upon us, because our fathers have not kept the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to do after all that is written in this book. <hi type="super">22</hi> And Hilkiah, and <hi type="italic">they</hi> that the king <hi type="italic">had appointed,</hi> went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvath, the son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college:) and they spake to her to that <hi type="italic">effect.</hi> <hi type="super">23</hi> And she answered them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, Tell ye the man that sent you to me, <hi type="super">24</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, and upon the inhabitants thereof, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all the curses that are written in the book which they have read before the king of Judah: <hi type="super">25</hi> Because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the works of their hands; therefore my wrath shall be poured out upon this place, and shall not be quenched. <hi type="super">26</hi> And as for the king of Judah, who sent you to enquire of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , so shall ye say unto him, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> the words which thou hast heard; <hi type="super">27</hi> Because thine heart was tender, and thou didst humble thyself before God, when thou heardest his words against this place, and against the inhabitants thereof, and humbledst thyself before me, and didst rend thy clothes, and weep before me; I have even heard <hi type="italic">thee</hi> also, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">28</hi> Behold, I will gather thee to thy fathers, and thou shalt be gathered to thy grave in peace, neither shall thine eyes see all the evil that I will bring upon this place, and upon the inhabitants of the same. So they brought the king word again. <div eID="gen8488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8489" type="x-p"/> This whole paragraph we had, just as it is here related, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.8-2Kgs.22.20">2 Kings xxii. 8-20</reference>, and have nothing to add here to what was there observed. But, 1. We may hence take occasion to bless God that we have plenty of Bibles, and that they are, or may be, in all hands,—that the book of the law and gospel is not lost, is not scarce,—that, in this sense, the <hi type="italic">word of the Lord</hi> is not <hi type="italic">precious.</hi> Bibles are jewels, but, thanks be to God, they are not rarities. The fountain of the waters of life is not a spring shut up or a fountain sealed, but the streams of it, in all places, <hi type="italic">make glad the city of our God. Usus communis aquarum—These waters flow for general use.</hi> What a great deal shall we have to answer for if the great things of God's law, being thus made common, should be accounted by us as strange things! 2. We may hence learn, whenever we read or hear the word of God, to affect our hearts with it, and to get them possessed with a holy fear of that wrath of God which is there revealed against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, as Josiah's tender heart was. When he heard the words of the law he <hi type="italic">rent his clothes</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.19">v. 19</reference>), and God was well pleased with his doing so, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.27">v. 27</reference>. Were the things contained in the scripture new to us, as they were here to Josiah, surely they would make deeper impressions upon us than commonly they do; but they are not the less weighty, and therefore should not be the less considered by us, for their being well known. Rend the heart therefore, not the garments. 3. We are here directed when we are under convictions of sin, and apprehensions of divine wrath, to enquire of the Lord; so Josiah did, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.21">v. 21</reference>. It concerns us to ask (as they did, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.37">Acts ii. 37</reference>), <hi type="italic">Men and brethren, what shall we do?</hi> and more particularly (as the jailor), <hi type="italic">What must I do to be saved?</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.16.30">Acts xvi. 30</reference>. <hi type="italic">If you will</hi> thus <hi type="italic">enquire, enquire</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.12">Isa. xxi. 12</reference>); and, blessed be God, we have the lively oracles to which to apply with these enquiries. 4. We are here warned of the ruin that sin brings upon nations and kingdoms. Those that forsake God bring evil upon themselves (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.24-2Chr.34.25">v. 24, 25</reference>), and kindle a fire <hi type="italic">which shall not be quenched.</hi> Such will the fire of God's wrath be when the decree has gone forth against those that obstinately and impenitently persist in their wicked ways. 5. We are here encouraged to humble ourselves before God and seek unto him, as Josiah did. If we cannot prevail thereby to turn away God's wrath from our land, yet we shall deliver our own souls, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.27-2Chr.34.28">v. 27, 28</reference>. And good people are here taught to be so far from fearing death as to welcome it rather when it <hi type="italic">takes them away from the evil to come.</hi> See how the property of it is altered by making it the matter of a promise: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be gathered to thy grave in peace,</hi> housed in that ark, as Noah, when a deluge is coming.
entries.f40fe0c06ccfe9a3c4ed2d8aa17a1f024e6833bf: <div eID="gen8489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8490" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> Then the king sent and gathered together all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. <hi type="super">30</hi> And the king went up into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and all the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the priests, and the Levites, and all the people, great and small: and he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant that was found in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">31</hi> And the king stood in his place, and made a covenant before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to walk after the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and to keep his commandments, and his testimonies, and his statutes, with all his heart, and with all his soul, to perform the words of the covenant which are written in this book. <hi type="super">32</hi> And he caused all that were present in Jerusalem and Benjamin to stand <hi type="italic">to it.</hi> And the inhabitants of Jerusalem did according to the covenant of God, the God of their fathers. <hi type="super">33</hi> And Josiah took away all the abominations out of all the countries that <hi type="italic">pertained</hi> to the children of Israel, and made all that were present in Israel to serve, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to serve the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God. <hi type="italic">And</hi> all his days they departed not from following the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of their fathers. <div eID="gen8490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8491" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the further advances which Josiah made towards the reformation of his kingdom upon the hearing of the law read and the receipt of the message God sent him by the prophetess. Happy the people that had such a king; for here we find that, 1. They were well taught. He did not go about to force them to do their duty, till he had first instructed them in it. He called all the people together, great and small, young and old, rich and poor, high and low. <hi type="italic">He that hath ears to hear, let him hear</hi> the words of <hi type="italic">the book of the covenant;</hi> for they are all concerned in those words. To put an honour upon the service, and to engage attention the more, though there were priests and Levites present, the king himself read the book to the people (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.30">v. 30</reference>), and he read it, no doubt, in such a manner as to show that he was himself affected with it, which would be a means of affecting the hearers. 2. They were well fixed. The articles of agreement between God and Israel being read, that they might intelligently covenant with God, both king and people with great solemnity did as it were subscribe the articles. The king in his place covenanted to keep God's commandments with all his heart and soul, according to what was <hi type="italic">written in the book</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.31">v. 31</reference>), and urged the people to declare their consent likewise to this covenant, and solemnly to promise that they would faithfully perform, fulfil, and keep, all and every thing that was on their part to be done, according to this covenant: this they did; they could not for shame do otherwise. He caused <hi type="italic">all that were present</hi> to <hi type="italic">stand to it</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.32">v. 32</reference>), and made them all <hi type="italic">to serve, even to serve the Lord their God</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.33">v. 33</reference>), to do it and to <hi type="italic">make a business</hi> of it. He did all he could to bring them to it—<hi type="italic">to serve, even to serve;</hi> the repetition denotes that this was the only thing his heart was set on; he aimed at nothing else in what he did but to engage them to God and their duty. 3. They were well tended, were honest with good looking to. <hi type="italic">All his days they departed not from following the Lord;</hi> he kept them, with much ado, from running into idolatry again. <hi type="italic">All his days</hi> were days of restraint upon them; but this intimated that there was in them a <hi type="italic">bent to backslide,</hi> a strong inclination to idolatry. Many of them wanted nothing but to have him out of the way, and then they would have their high places and their images up again. And therefore we find that <hi type="italic">in the days of Josiah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.6">Jer. iii. 6</reference>) God charged it upon treacherous Judah that she <hi type="italic">had not returned to him with all her heart, but feignedly</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.10">v. 10</reference>), nay, had <hi type="italic">played the harlot</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.8">v. 8</reference>) and thereby had even <hi type="italic">justified backsliding Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.11">v. 11</reference>. In the twenty-third year of this reign, four or five years after this, they had <hi type="italic">gone on to provoke God to anger with the works of their hands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.3-Jer.25.7">Jer. xxv. 3-7</reference>); and, which is very observable, it is from the beginning of Josiah's reformation, his twelfth or thirteenth year, that <hi type="italic">the iniquity of the house of Judah,</hi> which brought ruin upon them, and which the prophet was to bear lying on his right side, was dated (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.6">Ezek. iv. 6</reference>), for thence to the destruction of Jerusalem was just forty years. Josiah was sincere in what he did, but the generality of the people were averse to it and hankered after their idols still; so that the reformation, though well designed and well prosecuted by the prince, had little or no effect upon the people. It was with reluctancy that they parted with their idols; still they were in heart joined to them, and wished for them again. This God saw, and therefore from that time, when one would have thought the foundations had been laid for a perpetual security and peace, from that very time did the decree go forth for their destruction. Nothing hastens the ruin of a people nor ripens them for it more than the baffling of hopeful attempts for reformation and a hypocritical return to God. <hi type="italic">Be not deceived, God is not mocked.</hi>  <chapter eID="2Chr.34"/> <div eID="gen8491" type="x-p"/>

entries.ae9f4d39c20757f0f57be2e8e8c0b4f4ccf47c8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4176"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 34</title> <div sID="gen6065" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.1">2Ch 34:1</reference>, 2. Josiah's Good Reign.<div eID="gen6065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6066" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4176"/><hi type="bold">1. Josiah was eight years old--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.1">2Ki 22:1</reference>). The testimony borne to the undeviating steadfastness of his adherence to the cause of true religion places his character and reign in honorable contrast with those of many of his royal predecessors.<div eID="gen6066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6067" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.3-2Chr.34.7">2Ch 34:3-7</reference>. He Destroys Idolatry. <div eID="gen6067" type="x-p"/>
entries.562183c90cf761b94b566bdd9de0e6c170c4e8f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4177"/><div sID="gen6068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4177"/><hi type="bold">3. in the eighth year of his reign--</hi>This was the sixteenth year of his age, and, as the kings of Judah were considered minors till they had completed their thirteenth year, it was three years after he had attained majority. He had very early manifested the piety and excellent dispositions of his character. In the twelfth year of his reign, but the twentieth of his age, he began to take a lively interest in the purgation of his kingdom from all the monuments of idolatry which, in his father's short reign, had been erected. At a later period, his increasing zeal for securing the purity of divine worship led him to superintend the work of demolition in various parts of his dominion. The course of the narrative in this passage is somewhat different from that followed in the Book of Kings. For the historian, having made allusion to the early manifestation of Josiah's zeal, goes on with a full detail of all the measures this good king adopted for the extirpation of idolatry; whereas the author of the Book of Kings sets out with the cleansing of the temple, immediately previous to the celebration of the passover, and embraces that occasion to give a general description of Josiah's policy for freeing the land from idolatrous pollution. The exact chronological order is not followed either in Kings or Chronicles. But it is clearly recorded in both that the abolition of idolatry began in the twelfth and was completed in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign. Notwithstanding Josiah's undoubted sincerity and zeal and the people's apparent compliance with the king's orders, he could not extinguish a strongly rooted attachment to idolatries introduced in the early part of Manasseh's reign. This latent predilection appears unmistakably developed in the subsequent reigns, and the divine decree for the removal of Judah, as well as Israel, into captivity was irrevocably passed. <div eID="gen6068" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd9540c2251b575bfa64d42864f15c03d5bb1a56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4178"/><div sID="gen6069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4178"/><hi type="bold">4. the graves of them that had sacrificed unto them--</hi>He treated the graves themselves as guilty of the crimes of those who were lying in them [Bertheau]. <div eID="gen6069" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea1925a4f86cb7bf7a14fcdff0372d970491e3d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4179"/><div sID="gen6070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4179"/><hi type="bold">5. he burnt the bones of the priests upon their altars--</hi>A greater brand of infamy could not have been put on idolatrous priests than the disinterment of their bones, and a greater defilement could not have been done to the altars of idolatry than the burning upon them the bones of those who had there officiated in their lifetime. <div eID="gen6070" type="x-p"/>
entries.84e8894c84508ae96c8d9bcb01b18c2653dad56c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4180"/><div sID="gen6071" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4180"/><hi type="bold">6. with their mattocks--</hi>or, "in their deserts"--so that the verse will stand thus: "And so did [namely, break the altars and burn the bones of priests] he in the cities of Manasseh, and Ephraim, and Simeon, even unto Naphtali, in their deserted suburbs." The reader is apt to be surprised on finding that Josiah, whose hereditary possessions were confined to the kingdom of Judah, exercised as much authority among the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, Simeon, and others as far as Naphtali, as he did within his own dominion. Therefore, it is necessary to observe that, after the destruction of Samaria by Shalmaneser, the remnant that continued on the mountains of Israel maintained a close intercourse with Judah, and looked to the sovereigns of that kingdom as their natural protectors. Those kings acquired great influence over them, which Josiah exercised in removing every vestige of idolatry from the land. He could not have done this without the acquiescence of the people in the propriety of this proceeding, conscious that this was conformable to their ancient laws and institutions. The Assyrian kings, who were now masters of the country, might have been displeased at the liberties Josiah took beyond his own territories. But either they were not informed of his doings, or they did not trouble themselves about his religious proceedings, relating, as they would think, to the god of the land, especially as he did not attempt to seize upon any place or to disturb the allegiance of the people [Calmet].<div eID="gen6071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6072" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.8-2Chr.34.18">2Ch 34:8-18</reference>. He Repairs the Temple. <div eID="gen6072" type="x-p"/>

entries.a791305152fa7b528f650bb77ff588de16694797: <div eID="gen14623" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14624" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14625" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14625" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14624" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14626" type="x-p"/> Josiah reigns thirty-one years; destroys idolatry in Judah, as also in Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and even to Naphtali, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.1-2Chr.34.7">2Chr 34:1-7</reference>. He begins to repair the temple, and collects money for the purpose, and employs workmen, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.8-2Chr.34.13">2Chr 34:8-13</reference>. Hilkiah the priest finds the book of the law in the temple, which is read by Shaphan before the king, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.14-2Chr.34.19">2Chr 34:14-19</reference>. He is greatly troubled, and consults Huldah the prophetess, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.20-2Chr.34.22">2Chr 34:20-22</reference>. Her exhortation, and message to the king, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.23-2Chr.34.28">2Chr 34:23-28</reference>. He causes it to be read to the elders of Judah, and they make a covenant with God, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.29">2Chr 34:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.32">2Chr 34:32</reference>. Josiah reforms every abomination, and the people serve God all his days, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.33">2Chr 34:33</reference>.
entries.3c52cd60b7112272375408411f9ae616b3343f74: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen14626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14627" type="x-p"/> He declined neither to the right hand, nor to the left - He never swerved from God and truth; he never omitted what he knew to be his duty to God and his kingdom; he carried on his reformation with a steady hand; timidity did not prevent him from going far enough; and zeal did not lead him beyond due bounds. He walked in the golden mean, and his moderation was known unto all men. He went neither to the right nor to the left, he looked inward, looked forward, and looked upward. Reader, let the conduct of this pious youth be thy exemplar through life.
entries.e3ef2561f51d2ebfb6ac8cc95e0399192c35c172: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen14627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14628" type="x-p"/> The altars of Baalim - How often have these been broken down, and how soon set up again! We see that the religion of a land is as the religion of its king. If the king were idolatrous, up went the altars, on them were placed the statues, and the smoke of incense ascended in ceaseless clouds to the honor of that which is vanity, and nothing to the world; on the other hand, when the king was truly religious, down went the idolatrous altars, broken in pieces were the images, and the sacrificial smoke ascended only to the true God: in all these cases the people were as one man with the king.
entries.063fcef83776a1d9c48812488b2327887d2e7a9a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen14628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14629" type="x-p"/> He burnt the bones of the priests - כומריא kumeraiya, the kemarim, says the Targum. See this word explained, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">2Kgs 23:5</reference> (note).
entries.5feb43c2ad961aa6c35cc3c047a2ac7e61b3ed48: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen14629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14630" type="x-p"/> The cities of Manasseh - Even those who were under the government of the Israelitish king permitted their idols and places of idolatry to be hewn down and destroyed: after the truth was declared and acknowledged, the spade and the axe were employed to complete the reformation.
entries.ceb17a81e8b0aee28304cd7a03c56c5fbec864fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen14630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14631" type="x-p"/> And they returned to Jerusalem - Instead of וישבו vaiyashubu, "they returned," we should read יושבי yoshebey, "the inhabitants;" a reading which is supported by many MSS., printed editions, and all the versions, as well as by necessity and common sense. See the note on <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.8">2Chr 19:8</reference>, where a similar mistake is rectified.
entries.2c300ecae242ddb4974f45bb409e3a1b124cb364: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen14631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14632" type="x-p"/> All that could skill of instruments of music - Did the musicians play on their several instruments to encourage and enliven the workmen? Is not this a probable case from their mention here? If this were really the case, instrumental music was never better applied in any thing that refers to the worship of God. It is fabled of Orpheus, a most celebrated musician, that such was the enchanting harmony of his lyre, that he built the city of Thebes by it: the stones and timbers danced to his melody; and by the power of his harmony rose up, and took their respective places in the different parts of the wall that was to defend the city! This is fable; but as all fable is a representation of truth, where is the truth and fact to which this refers? How long has this question lain unanswered! But have we not the answer now? It is known in general, that the cities of Herculaneum and Pompeii were overwhelmed by an eruption of Mount Vesuvius, about the seventy-ninth year of the Christian era. It is also known that, in sinking for wells, the workmen of the king of Naples lighted on houses, etc., of those overwhelmed cities; that excavations have been carried on, and are now in the act of being carried on, which are bringing daily to view various utensils, pictures, and books, which have escaped the influence of the burning lava; and that some of those parchment volumes have been unrolled, and facsimiles of them engraved and published; and that our late Prince Regent, afterwards George IV., king of Great Britain, expended considerable sums of money annually in searching for, unrolling, and deciphering those rolls. This I record to his great credit as the lover of science and literature. Now, among the books that have been unrolled and published, is a Greek Treatise on Music, by Philodemus; and here we have the truth represented which lay hidden under the fables of Orpheus and Amphion. This latter was a skillful harper, who was frequently employed by the Theban workmen to play to them while engaged in their labor, and for which they rewarded him out of the proceeds of that labor. So powerful and pleasing was his music, that they went lightly and comfortably through their work; and time and labor passed on without tedium or fatigue; and the walls and towers were speedily raised. This, by a metaphor, was attributed to the dulcet sounds of his harp; and poetry seized on and embellished it, and mythology incorporated it with her fabulous system. Orpheus is the same. By his skill in music he drew stones and trees after him, i.e., he presided over and encouraged the workmen by his skill in music. Yet how simple and natural is the representation given by this ancient Greek writer of such matters! See Philodemus, Col. viii. and ix. Orpheus, and Amphion, by their music, moved the workmen to diligence and activity, and lessened and alleviated their toil. May we not suppose, then, that skillful musicians among the Levites did exercise their art among the workmen who were employed in the repairs of the house of the Lord? May I be allowed a gentle transition? Is it not the power and harmony of the grace of Jesus Christ in the Gospel, that convert, change, and purify the souls of men, and prepare them for and place them in that part of the house of God, the New Jerusalem? A most beautiful and chaste allusion to this fact and fable is made by an eminent poet, while praying for his own success as a Christian minister, who uses all his skill as a poet and musician for the glory of God: - <div eID="gen14632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14633" type="x-p"/> Thy own musician, Lord, inspire, <div eID="gen14633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14634" type="x-p"/> And may my consecrated lyre <div eID="gen14634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14635" type="x-p"/> Repeat the psalmist's part! <div eID="gen14635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14636" type="x-p"/> His Son and thine reveal in me, <div eID="gen14636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14637" type="x-p"/> And fill with sacred melody <div eID="gen14637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14638" type="x-p"/> The fibres of my heart. <div eID="gen14638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14639" type="x-p"/> So shall I charm the listening throng, <div eID="gen14639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14640" type="x-p"/> And draw the Living Stones along <div eID="gen14640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14641" type="x-p"/> By Jesus' tuneful name. <div eID="gen14641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14642" type="x-p"/> The living stones shall dance, shall rise, <div eID="gen14642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14643" type="x-p"/> And Form a City in the skies, <div eID="gen14643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14644" type="x-p"/> The New Jerusalem. <div eID="gen14644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14645" type="x-p"/> Charles Wesley.

entries.4477c9403abee67d9e5bd831914243a90ef20c95: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen14647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14648" type="x-p"/> Because thine heart was tender - "Because thy heart was melted, and thou hast humbled thyself in the sight of the Word of the Lord, מימרא דיי meymera daya, when thou didst hear his words, ית פתגמוי yath pithgamoi, against this place," etc. Here the Targum most evidently distinguishes between מימרא meymera, the Personal Word, and פתגם pithgam, a word spoken or expressed.

entries.a94c1870523c2133d64e1eceee44fce4ed66daf9: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen14651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14652" type="x-p"/> To stand to it - It is likely that he caused them all to arise when he read the terms of the covenant, and thus testify their approbation of the covenant itself, and their resolution to observe it faithfully and perseveringly.  <chapter eID="2Chr.34"/> <div eID="gen14652" type="x-p"/>

entries.ade3bfe44c87f756f17455f5168716fca358af6c: <div eID="gen6232" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Reign of Josiah - 2 Chronicles 34-35</title> <div sID="gen6233" type="x-p"/> The account of Josiah in the Chronicle agrees in all essential points with the representation in 2 Kings 22 and 23, but is chronologically more exact, and in many parts more complete than that. In the second book of Kings, the whole reform of the cultus carried out by Josiah is viewed in its connection with the discovery of the book of the law, on the occasion of the temple being repaired; and the narrative comprehends not only the repair of the temple, the discovery, the reading of the book of the law before the assembled people, and the renewal of the covenant, but also the extirpation of idolatry in Jerusalem and Judah and in all the cities of Israel, and the celebration of the passover in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign; see the introductory remarks to 2 Kings 22. In the Chronicle, on the contrary, these events are more kept apart, and described according to their order in time. As early as in the eighth year of his reign, Josiah, still a youth, began to seek the God of his ancestor David, and in his twelfth year to purge Jerusalem and Judah of idolatry (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.3">2Ch 34:3</reference>). In the eighteenth year the book of the law was discovered in the temple, brought to the king, and read before him (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.8-2Chr.34.18">2Ch 34:8-18</reference>); whereupon he, deeply moved by the contents of the book which had been read, and by the answer of the prophetess Huldah when inquired of concerning it (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.19-2Chr.34.28">2Ch 34:19-28</reference>), went into the temple with the elders of the people, caused the law to be read to the whole people, and made a covenant before the Lord to obey the law (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.29-2Chr.34.32">2Ch 34:29-32</reference>). He then caused all the idolatrous abominations which were still to be found in the land of Israel to be removed (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.33">2Ch 34:33</reference>), and prepared to hold the passover, as it had not been held since the days of Solomon (2 Chron 35:1-19). In other respects the main difference between the two accounts is, that in 2 Kings the suppression of idolatry is narrated with greater minuteness; the passover, on the contrary, being only briefly noticed; - while in the Chronicle the purification of Jerusalem, Judah, and the kingdom of Israel is shortly summarized (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.3-2Chr.34.7">2Ch 34:3-7</reference>), but the celebration of the passover is minutely described on its ceremonial side (2 Chron 35:1-19). <div eID="gen6233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6234" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.1-2Chr.34.2">2Ch 34:1-2</reference> <hi type="italic">Duration and spirit of Josiah’s reign;</hi> agreeing with 2Ki 22:1, 2Ki 22:2, only the note as to Josiah’s mother being here omitted.
entries.f1c190cc8a3b8a4a89aa932be5455991b20d00f7: <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.3-2Chr.34.4">2Ch 34:3-4</reference> <hi type="italic">Extirpation of idolatry</hi>. In the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet a youth, being then only sixteen years old, Josiah began to seek the God of his ancestor David, and in the twelfth year of his reign he commenced to purify Judah and Jerusalem from the high places, Asherim, etc. The cleansing of the land of Judah from the numerous objects of idolatry is summarily described in <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.4">2Ch 34:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.5">2Ch 34:5</reference>; and thereupon there follows (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.6">2Ch 34:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.7">2Ch 34:7</reference>) the destruction of the idolatrous altars and images in the land of Israel, - all that it seemed necessary to say on that subject being thus mentioned at once. For that all this was not accomplished in the twelfth year is clear from the לטהר החל, “he commenced to cleanse,” and is moreover attested by 2Ch 34:33. The description of this destruction of the various objects of idolatry is rhetorically expressed, only carved and cast images being mentioned, besides the altars of the high places and the Asherim, without the enumeration of the different kings of idolatry which we find in 2 Kings 23:4-20. - On <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.4">2Ch 34:4</reference>, cf. 2Ch 31:1. ינתּציּ, they pulled down before him, i.e., under his eye, or his oversight, the altars of the Baals (these are the בּמות, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.3">2Ch 34:3</reference>); and the sun-pillars (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.4">2Ch 14:4</reference>) which stood upwards, i.e., above, upon the altars, he caused to be hewn away from them (מעליהם); the Asherim (pillars and trees of Asherah) and the carved and molten images to be broken and ground (הדק, cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.16">2Ch 15:16</reference>), and (the dust of them) to be strewn upon the graves (of those) who had sacrificed to them. הזּבחים is connected directly with הקּברים, so that the actions of those buried in them are poetically attributed to the graves. In 2Ki 23:6 this is said only of the ashes of the Asherah statue which was burnt, while here it is rhetorically generalized.
entries.4cb96b7e4a759c29f6706851d12383b192de73c3: <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.5">2Ch 34:5</reference> <div eID="gen6234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6235" type="x-p"/> And he burnt the bones of the priests upon their altars, i.e., he caused the bones of the idolatrous priests to be taken from their graves and burnt on the spot where the destroyed altars had stood, that he might defile the place with the ashes of the dead. In these words is summarized what is stated in 2Ki 23:13 and 2Ki 23:14 as to the defilement of the places of sacrifice built upon the Mount of Olives by the bones of the dead, and in 2Ki 23:16-20 as to the burning of the bones of the high priests of Bethel, after they had been taken from their graves, upon their own altars. מזבחותים is an orthographical error for מזבּחותם.
entries.7edf061eed46eb35af235c01df34beefc0c77901: <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.6-2Chr.34.7">2Ch 34:6-7</reference> <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.6">2Ch 34:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.7">2Ch 34:7</reference> form a connected sentence: And in the cities of Manasseh ..., in their ruins round about, there he pulled down the altars, etc. The tribe of Simeon is here, as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.9">2Ch 15:9</reference>, reckoned among the tribes of the kingdom of Israel, because the Simeonites, although they belonged geographically to the kingdom of Judah, yet in religion remained attached to the worship on the high places practised by the ten tribes; see on 2Ch 15:9. “And unto Naphtali” is added, to designate the kingdom of Israel in its whole extent to the northern frontier of Canaan. The form בתיהם בּחר (in the Keth. divided into two words) gives no suitable sense. R. Sal. explains, <hi type="italic">timentes in planitie habitare, sed fixerunt in monte domicilia,</hi> rendering it “in their mountain-dwellings.” This the words cannot mean.<note placement="foot">The lxx translate ἐν τοῖς τόποις αὐτῶν, expressing merely the בתיהם. The Targ. has צדיוּתהון בבית, <hi type="italic">in domo</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. loco</hi>) <hi type="italic">desolationis eorum</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen6235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6236" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> בּחרבתיהם, “with their swords,” is suggested by <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.9">Eze 26:9</reference>, and is accepted by D. Kimchi, Abu Melech, and others, and understood to denote instruments with which the altars, groves, and images were cut down. But this interpretation also is certainly incorrect. The word is rather to be pointed בּחרבתיהם, in their wastes (ruins) (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.109.10">Psa 109:10</reference>), and to be taken as an explanatory apposition to בּערי: in the cities of Manasseh ..., namely, in their ruins round about; for the land had been deserted since the times of Shalmaneser, and its cities were in great part in ruins. The statement as to the locality precedes in the form of an absolute sentence, and that which is predicated of it follows in the form of an apodosis with ו <hi type="italic">consec</hi>. (וינתּץ). להדק כּתּת, he dashed to pieces to crush; the form הדק is not a perfect after ל, but an infinitive which has retained the vowel of the perfect; cf. Ew. §238, <hi type="italic">d</hi>.
entries.560a2fc74dea0c083577ad77653175f1762c1225: <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.8">2Ch 34:8</reference> <hi type="italic">The cleansing and repairing of the temple, and the finding of the book of the law</hi>. Cf. 2Ki 22:3-10. - In the eighteenth year of his reign, when he was purging the land and the house (of God), he sent. לטהר does not indeed signify “after the purging” (De Wette, with the older expositors), but still less is it a statement of the object, “to purge” (Berth.); for that is decisively disposed of both by its position at the beginning of the sentence, where no statement of the object would stand, but still more by the fact that a statement of the object follows, וגו לחזּק.   ל used of time denotes “about,” and so with the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>., e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.46.13">Jer 46:13</reference> : at (his) coming = when he came. Shaphan was סופר, state secretary, according to 2Ki 22:3. With him the king sent the governor of the city Maaseiah, and the chancellor Joah. These two are not mentioned in 2Ki 22:3, but have not been arbitrarily added by the chronicler, or invented by him, as Then. groundlessly supposes. “To repair the house of Jahve.” What these high royal officials had to do with it we learn from what follows.
entries.789d67e79735c9f59163d5dee31a5a82f4d42c25: <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.9-2Chr.34.12">2Ch 34:9-12</reference> <div eID="gen6236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6237" type="x-p"/> They, together with the high priest, gave the money which had been received for the repair of the temple to the overseers of the building, who then gave it to workmen to procure building materials and for wages, just as was done when the temple was repaired by Joash, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.11">2Ch 24:11</reference>-13. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> ויּשׁבוּ is a correction resulting from a misinterpretation of the Keth. וישׁבי, “and of the dwellers in Jerusalem.” The enumeration, “from the hand of Manasseh, Ephraim,” etc., is rhetorical. In ויּתּנוּ, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.10">2Ch 34:10</reference>, the verb of <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.9">2Ch 34:9</reference> is again taken up: they handed it to the overseers of the building, and they to the workmen. הם עשׂה is a rare form of the plur. עשׁי; see on 1Ch 23:24. The overseers of the building (המפקדים - עשׁי) are the subject of the second ויּתּנוּ; and before the following עשׂי ל, which stands in 2 Kings, is to be supplied. בדוק is a denom. from בּדק, and signifies to repair what has been damaged. The statement of <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.10">2Ch 34:10</reference> is made more definite by <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.11">2Ch 34:11</reference> : they gave it, namely, to the workers in stone and wood, and to the builders to buy hewn stones and timber for couplings, and for the beams of the houses (לקרות, to provide with beams; הבּתים are the various buildings of the temple and its courts), which the kings of Judah had allowed to decay (השׁחית, not of designed destroying, but of ruining by neglect). - In <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.12">2Ch 34:12</reference> we have still the remark that the people did the work with fidelity, and the money could consequently be given to them without reckoning, cf. 2Ki 22:7; and then the names of the building inspectors follow. Two Levites of the family of Merari, and two of the family of Kohath, were overseers; לנצּח, i.e., to lead in the building, to preside over it as upper overseers; and besides them, the Levites, all who were skilled in instruments of song (cf. 1Ch 25:6.). As men who by their office and their art occupied a conspicuous place among the Levites, the oversight of the workmen in the temple was committed to them, not “that they might incite and cheer the workmen by music and song” (Berth.).
entries.c97f3085686b7e9e705e1b0cdd105b5103138a2f: <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.13">2Ch 34:13</reference> <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.13">2Ch 34:13</reference> is probably to be taken, along with <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.12">2Ch 34:12</reference>, in the signification, “All the Levites who were skilled in music were over the bearers of burdens, and were overseers of all the workmen in reference to every work.” The ו before הס על appears certainly to go against this interpretation, and Berth. would consequently erase it to connect הסּבּלים על with the preceding verse, and begin a new sentence with וּמנצּחים: “and they led all the workmen.” But if we separate וּמנצּחים from הסּבּלים על, this mention of the bearers of burdens (סבלים) comes awkwardly in between the subject and the predicate, or the statement as to the subject. We hold the text to be correct, and make the w before הס על correspond to the ו before מנצחים, in the signification, <hi type="italic">et</hi> - <hi type="italic">et</hi>. The Levites, all who were skilled in instruments of song, were both over the bearers of burdens, and overseeing the workmen, or leading the workmen. Besides, of the Levites were, i.e., still other Levites were, scribes and officers and porters, i.e., were busied about the temple in the discharge of these functions.
entries.b689fa04fade5f4737c402e3930494a3c434d21d: <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.14-2Chr.34.18">2Ch 34:14-18</reference> <div eID="gen6237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6238" type="x-p"/> In bringing out the money that had been brought into the house of the Lord, the high priest found the book of Moses’ law. It is not clearly implied in the words, that he found it in the place where the money was laid up. The book of the law which was found is merely characterized as the book of the Mosaic law by the words בּיד־משׁה, not necessarily as Moses’ autograph. The communication of this discovery by the high priest to the state secretary Shaphan, and by him to the king, is narrated in <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.15-2Chr.34.18">2Ch 34:15-18</reference>, just as in 2Ki 22:8-10. The statement, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.16">2Ch 34:16</reference>, “And Shaphan brought the book to the king,” instead of the words, “and Shaphan the ספר came (went) to the king,” involves no difference as to the facts; it rather makes the matter clear. For since in 2Ki 22:10, immediately after the statement that Hilkiah gave him the book, it is said that Shaphan read from it to the king, he must have brought it to the king. With this elucidation, both the omission of ויּקראהוּ   (2Ki 22:8), and the insertion of עוד after ויּשׁב, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.16">2Ch 34:16</reference>, is connected. The main thing, that which it concerned the author of the Chronicle to notice, was the fact that the book of the law which had been discovered was immediately brought and read to the king; while the circumstance that Shaphan, when the book was given him, also opened it and read in it, is omitted, as it had no further results. But since Shaphan did not go to the king merely to bring him the book, but rather, in the first place, to report upon the performance of the commission entrusted to him in respect of the money, this report required to be brought prominently forward by the עוד: He brought the book to the king, and besides, made his report to the king. All that has been committed to thy servants (בּיד נתן), that they do; they have poured out the money, etc. The עבדים are not Shaphan and the others mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.8">2Ch 34:8</reference>, but in general those who were entrusted with the oversight of the repair of the temple, among whom, indeed, the chief royal officials were not included. After this report there follows in <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.18">2Ch 34:18</reference> an account of the book which Shaphan had brought, and which, as we were informed in <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.16">2Ch 34:16</reference>, in anticipation of the event, he gave to the king.
entries.5d9fecfe0fe15c414527916d96f98feb70b57dfd: <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.19-2Chr.34.28">2Ch 34:19-28</reference> <hi type="italic">The dismay of the king at the contents of the book which was read to him, and his inquiry of the prophetess Huldah as to the judgments threatened in the law</hi>. - Compare with this the parallel account in 2Ki 22:11-20, with the commentary there given, as both accounts agree with the exception of some unimportant variations in expression. Instead of Abdon ben Micah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.20">2Ch 34:20</reference>) we find in 2 Kings Achbor ben Micayahu, perhaps the correct reading. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.21">2Ch 34:21</reference>, the expression, “and for those that are left in Israel and Judah,” i.e., for the remainder of the people who were left in Israel after the destruction of the kingdom, and in Judah after the divine chastisements inflicted, mainly by the Assyrians under Hezekiah and Manasseh, is clearer and more significant than that in 2Ki 22:13, “and for the people, and for all Judah.” נתּכה, to pour itself forth (of anger), is quite as suitable as נצּתה, inflame, kindle itself, in 2Ki 22:13. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.22">2Ch 34:22</reference>, those sent with the high priest Hilkiah are briefly designated by the words המּלך ואשׁר, and whom the king, <hi type="italic">scil.</hi> had sent; in 2Ki 22:14, on the contrary, the individual names are recorded (Ewald, <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. §292, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, would supply אמר, after the lxx). The names of the ancestors of the prophetess Huldah also are somewhat different. כּזאת, as the king had said to him, is omitted in 2 Kings. - In <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.24">2Ch 34:24</reference>, כּל־האלות, all the curses, is more significant than כּל־דּברי,   2Ki 22:16. ותּתּך (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.25">2Ch 34:25</reference>) is a statement of the result of the עזבוּני: Because they have forsaken me, my anger pours itself forth. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.27">2Ch 34:27</reference>, the rhetorical expansion of the words which God had spoken of Jerusalem in the law, וגו לשׁמּה להיות, inserted in 2Ki 22:19 as an elucidation, are omitted. After the preceding designation of these words as “the curses written in the law,” any further elucidation was superfluous. On the contents of the saying of the prophetess Huldah, see the commentary on 2Ki 22:16.
entries.2495f5cfffbb6923ed138a7d8a44ac35f319ee53: <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.29-2Chr.34.32">2Ch 34:29-32</reference> <hi type="italic">The reading of the book of the law in the temple, and the solemn renewal of the covenant,</hi> to which the king assembled the elders of Judah and Jerusalem, with all the people, after the saying of the prophetess Huldah had been reported to him, are recorded in 2Ki 23:1-3 as they are in the Chronicle, and have been commented upon at the former passage. Only <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.32">2Ch 34:32</reference>, the contents of which correspond to the words, “And the whole people entered into the covenant” (2Ki 23:3), will need explanation. ויּעמד is usually translated, “he caused the people to enter into the covenant” (after 2 Kings). This is in substance correct, but exegetically cannot be defended, since בּבּרית does not precede, so as to allow of its here being supplied from the context. ויּעמד only signifies, he caused all who were in Jerusalem and Benjamin to stand, and they did according to the covenant of God; whence we can easily supply in the first clause, “and to do according to the covenant.” The collocation, “in Jerusalem and in Benjamin,” is an abbreviation of the complete formula, “in Jerusalem and Judah and Benjamin;” then in the following clause only the inhabitants of Jerusalem are named as representatives of the inhabitants of the whole kingdom.
entries.d4d3cbd9067224c32b1299a2ad47a5aebc5a5901: <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.33">2Ch 34:33</reference> <div eID="gen6238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6239" type="x-p"/> But not only his own subjects did Josiah induce to act towards God in accordance with the covenant; in all the districts of the sons of Israel he removed the idolatrous abominations, and compelled every one in Israel to serve Jahve. The “sons of Israel,” as distinguished from the inhabitants of Jerusalem and Benjamin (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.32">2Ch 34:32</reference>), are the remnant of the ten tribes in their land, where Josiah, according to 2Ch 34:6., had also destroyed the idolatrous places of worship and the images. The statement in our verse, with which the account of Josiah’s cultus reform is concluded, refers to that. לעבד ויּעבד, he made to serve, compelled them to serve. By the abolition of idolatry he compelled them to worship Jahve. The last words of the verse are accordingly to be interpreted as signifying that Josiah, so long as he lived, allowed no open idolatry, but externally maintained the worship of Jahve. These measures could not effect a real, heartfelt conversion to God, and so the people fell again into open idolatry immediately after Josiah’s death; and Jeremiah continually complains of the defection and corruption of Judah and Israel: cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.1">2Ch 11:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.1">2Ch 13:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.1">2Ch 25:1</reference>, etc.<hi type="italic">The solemnization of the passover</hi>. - To ratify the renewal of the covenant, and to confirm the people in the communion with the Lord into which it had entered by the making of the covenant, Josiah, immediately after the finding of the book of the law and the renewal of the covenant, appointed a solemn passover to be held at the legal time, which is only briefly mentioned in 2Ki 23:21-23, but in the Chronicle is minutely described.  <chapter eID="2Chr.34"/> <div eID="gen6239" type="x-p"/>
